newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan economic reform plans seen positive.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan economic reform plans seen positive.

text.p: The Pakistani government's plans to stimulate growth and higher exports through supply side incentives were likely to have a positive impact in the longer run, a research report said.

"These reforms, if implemented effectively, should go a long way in resolving the stubborn fiscal imbalance which is the root cause of many of Pakistan's economic ills," ABN AMRO Bank said in a report received by Reuters on Friday.
"Whether the changes are able to provide a short-term dividend remains to be seen," it added.

Newspapers said Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz would unveil sweeping economic reforms in an address to the parliament on Friday, including radical cuts in taxes, tariffs and public spending to stimulate growth and exports.
The reforms follow the collapse of a standby loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund, suspended last week after Pakistan could not meet agreed targets.
The IMF has agreed to continue monitoring the economy and possibly start talks on a medium-term Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) programme later in the year.

ABN AMRO said the fact that these reforms were being formulated without IMF guidance should be taken as a signal of credibility and if the measures win IMF approval, preliminary negotiations for an ESAF could start even before the end of the fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).

"In fact, even a positive signal from the IMF will go a long way, in and of itself, to resolve the short-term uncertainty," it said, adding, Sharif's supply-side inclination will be put to the real test on the external imbalance front.
Bankers say Pakistan, with only a billion dollars in cash reserves, faces debt repayments worth $1.6 billion during the March-June period.
ABN AMRO said it expects the government to simplify the system of tax assessment and collection that will result in higher tax revenues even at reduced marginal tax rates.
The government is likely to extend the tax net to include the agriculture sector, which constitues almost 24 percent of the gross domestic product but has a minimal share in tax revenues.

The reforms may include granting the State (central) Bank of Pakistan its much-needed autonomy and a massive restructuring and subsequent privatisation plan for all state-run banks and financial institutions.
However, ABN AMRO said to boost aggregate supply without incurring a larger fiscal deficit was a tough feat to achieve.
It said efforts to boost production by reducing taxes and import duties on raw materials will reduce government revenues and could actually increase the trade imbalance.

The report said reducing or controlling input prices may provide greater comfort to local manufacturers, but the price distortions could extend coverage to inherently unviable units and encourage the establishment of an uncompetitive industry.

Encouraging production by providing or increasing export rebates not only entails a direct cost on the government, but efforts to subsidise exports will draw criticism and may lead exporters to complain of unfair trade practices, the report said.

The report said success of Sharif's strategy will depend on "whether the beneficiaries of this supply side boost will be able to increase and diversify Pakistan's export revenues and whether the government can adapt itself more strategically to promote Pakistan's exports in the new World Trade Order".
